summary: Defines a method for turning a name registered in the Domain Name System into an LDAP distinguished name. This gives directories a convenient way to name organizations based on their Internet domain names.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2247 gives a consistent way to write a DNS domain name as an LDAP directory name. Each part of the domain becomes a directory component, so the mapping can be reversed.

questions: how to represent a domain name as an ldap dn
what is dc in an ldap distinguished name
how to convert a domain name to an ldap dn
what is the dcobject object class
what is the domain object class in ldap
subtitle: A reversible rule for writing a DNS domain name as an LDAP distinguished name.

tldr.problem: LDAP needs a distinguished name for each directory entry, while DNS already provides a hierarchy of registered domain-name components.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2247 turns each domain component into a relative distinguished name whose attribute type is DC. It also defines the dc attribute and the dcObject and domain object classes.
tldr.outcome: An organization can derive directory names from domain names it already has. RFC 2247 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 4519 and RFC 4524.

today: RFC 2247 is a Proposed Standard published in January 1998. It has been updated by RFC 4519 and RFC 4524.

sections.title: Why Reuse Domain Names
sections.content:
LDAP identifies directory entries with X.500-compatible distinguished names (DNs). A DNS domain name is also a hierarchy, but its components do not carry the explicit attribute types that a DN requires.

X.500 does not require one naming structure, and the RFC notes that many regions lacked a system to assign unique names. Reusing a domain name gives an enterprise a directory name based on a name it has already registered. The memo does not define names for objects without domain names or how to locate an LDAP server from a domain name.
sections.plainLanguage: A directory name needs labels that say what each part means. This rule uses the parts of an existing Internet domain name to make that directory name.

sections.title: Turning Domain Components into DN Components
sections.content:
The conversion starts with an empty distinguished name. It adds one relative distinguished name for each domain component, beginning with the rightmost, most significant component. Each relative name contains a single attribute-value pair: the attribute type is DC, and the value is that domain component as an IA5 string.

For example, the RFC maps CS.UCL.AC.UK to DC=CS,DC=UCL,DC=AC,DC=UK. A distinguished name made from one or more relative names containing only DC can be converted back to a domain name. The rule defines no such conversion for other distinguished-name structures.
sections.plainLanguage: Take the domain's pieces from right to left and put DC before each one. The same steps in reverse recover the domain name.

sections.title: The dc Attribute
sections.content:
The attribute type dc means domainComponent. Its value holds one domain-name component, uses IA5 string syntax, and is single-valued. The RFC assigns it the object identifier 0.9.2342.19200300.100.1.25.

Equality and substring matching ignore letter case. This matches the case-insensitive behavior of DNS described in the RFC. In LDAP, the IA5 string is encoded as the characters of the component.
sections.plainLanguage: The dc attribute is one slot for one piece of a domain name. It treats uppercase and lowercase letters as equal.

sections.title: The dcObject and domain Classes
sections.content:
An LDAP object class controls which attributes an entry may contain. The auxiliary class dcObject permits and requires dc; it is added to an entry that already has a structural class, such as organization or locality. Its object identifier is 1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.344.

The structural class domain also requires dc. It is intended for entries without another suitable class, including placeholders. It permits optional descriptive attributes. The RFC also defines the X.500 name form domainNameForm, which names a domain entry using dc.
sections.plainLanguage: Use dcObject when a directory entry already describes an organization or another real entity. Use domain for a domain-name entry that has no other kind of object to describe.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says directory servers should maintain an appropriate security policy because clients can discover and retrieve object attributes. It also warns that enterprises may store information in DNS and LDAP without restrictions imposed by this naming rule.

A client that contacts an untrusted server may receive false or misleading information. A server could, for example, claim to hold naming contexts for domain names that were not delegated to it. The mapping itself does not verify that a server's claim is true.
sections.plainLanguage: A name that appears in a directory is not proof that the server has authority over it. Clients need to consider whether they trust the server that supplies the information.
